quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on sets, creels, cones, warper's and weaver's beams, and the bag of yarn that supplies them.

questions.q: In this lecture a 'set' is:
options: One full creel of cones warped onto the required number of warper's beams and then sized
One loom's production for a month
questions.explain: A set is the whole creel run off onto its warper's beams, which are then sized onto weaver's beams. A bag is the unit the yarn is issued in, not the set.

questions.q: What fixes the size of a set?
options: The length of yarn on one cone
questions.explain: Every end of the set comes from one cone, so the yardage one cone holds (less wastage) is the most that one set can warp for each end.

questions.q: How much yarn does one cone hold in the worksheet?
questions.explain: The cone size is 4.17 lb; 24 such cones make up a 100 lb bag. 24 lb and 100 lb describe the bag, not the cone.

questions.q: One 100 lb bag of yarn contains 24 cones of 4.17 lb.
questions.explain: 24 × 4.17 = 100.08 lb, which is why the bag count is ends per beam × sets ÷ 24.

questions.q: The total ends of a quality in the worksheet are calculated from:
questions.explain: 128 EPI × 63 in = 8,064 total ends for the first quality. Picks per inch is a weft figure and has nothing to do with the warp count.

questions.q: The 'Yd / sized beam' column in the worksheet is:
options: The length of yarn on one cone
The length of warp one weaver's beam can hold, found from the beam volume
The length of one warper's beam
The length of cloth per loom per day
questions.explain: The sized (weaver's) beam length comes from the beam volume and the yarn diameter: yarn cross-section × ends × length cannot exceed the beam's volume. One loom gets one such beam.

questions.q: Which formula gives the yarn diameter used in the beam-volume calculation?
questions.explain: d = 1/(26√Ne) inches; for Ne 20 this is about 0.0086 in. Option 1 is the formula turned upside down and would give a diameter of over 100 inches.

questions.q: 'Sets used' differs from the calculated 'Sets' because:
options: Sets are always rounded up to the next whole number
The fraction is rounded to a whole number with a 0.05 allowance, so 2.03 becomes 2 and the beams come out slightly shorter
Sets are halved to save yarn
The customer decides the number of sets
questions.explain: A set must be whole, but 2.03 is treated as 2 — the warper's beams simply carry a little less length. Only 2.06 or more would be rounded up to 3.

questions.q: Wastage of 2 % in the cone-length formula allows for:
options: Yarn lost in warping, sizing and the remnant left on each cone
questions.explain: The usable length per cone is reduced by 2 % for the yarn that cannot be warped — tails, knots and the remnant on the cone. Weft and cloth losses are counted elsewhere.

questions.q: Why does the 30/2 × 40/2 quality use Ne 15 as the warp count in the worksheet?
options: Because 30/2 is a two-ply yarn whose resultant count is 30 ÷ 2 = 15
Because 15 is the average of 30 and 2
Because folded yarns are counted in tex
questions.explain: Two singles of Ne 30 twisted together weigh twice as much per length, so the resultant count is Ne 15; the cone of 4.17 lb therefore holds only 51,491 yd.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The chain from cone to set to bags, and which way each figure moves when the count, cone size, loom number or beam volume changes.

questions.q: Length of yarn per cone, in yards, is:
questions.explain: One pound of Ne N yarn is 840 × N yards, so 4.17 lb of Ne 20 is 4.17 × 840 × 20 = 70,056 yd, less 2 % = 68,655 yd. Dividing by Ne would make finer yarn shorter, the reverse of the truth.

questions.q: The number of sets required for a quality is:
options: Beams × looms × sized length per beam ÷ length per cone
Length per cone ÷ sized length per beam
questions.explain: Each of the beams in the set must carry enough for all the looms' sized beams; that yardage divided by what a cone supplies gives the sets. Ends per beam ÷ 24 belongs to the bag formula.

questions.q: Bags of yarn to issue for a quality are:
questions.explain: Each set needs one cone per end on the creel, i.e. ends per beam cones; multiply by sets and divide by the 24 cones in a bag. Using total ends would count every beam's worth of cones separately.

questions.q: If the warp count changes from Ne 20 to Ne 30 (same cone weight), the length per cone will:
questions.explain: Length is proportional to Ne: 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 times as long, 102,982 yd instead of 68,655 yd for a 4.17 lb cone at 2 % wastage.

questions.q: For the same number of ends and the same beam volume, a finer yarn allows:
options: A longer sized beam, in proportion to Ne
questions.explain: The yarn cross-section is proportional to d², and d² = 1/(676 Ne), so the length that fits in the beam is proportional to Ne. Rows 7 and 8 show 2,198 yd at Ne 16 against 2,748 yd at Ne 20.

questions.q: Doubling the number of looms on a quality, everything else unchanged, will:
options: Double the sets required and roughly double the bags
Leave the sets unchanged but double the beams
questions.explain: Yards to size per warper's beam = sized length × looms, so the cone yardage required and the sets double; bags follow sets. Ends per beam depend on the quality, not on the looms.

questions.q: Increasing the beam volume lets each weaver's beam carry a longer warp and so reduces the number of sets for a given number of looms.
questions.explain: A longer sized beam means more yards to warp for each loom, so more cone yardage and more sets, not fewer. Fewer, longer beams reduce beam changes on the loom, which is a separate benefit.

questions.q: 'Actual yd / beam' in the worksheet is calculated as:
options: Yd per cone × sets used ÷ beams
questions.explain: The yardage the cones actually supply per end (yd per cone × whole sets) is shared over the beams of the set: 68,655 × 2 ÷ 10 = 13,731 yd, slightly less than the 13,911 yd wanted.

questions.q: How does the worksheet decide the beams per set?
options: Enough beams that no beam carries more than about 840 ends, rounded up to an even number
questions.explain: 8,064 ends ÷ 840 = 9.6, rounded up to 10 beams of 807 ends; 6,528 ends give 8 beams of 816. The even-number rule is a sizing-machine convention (beams are stacked in pairs).

questions.q: Ends per beam in the worksheet is:
questions.explain: 8,064 ÷ 10 = 806.4, rounded up to 807 so that the beams together cover all the ends; 840 is the ceiling used to choose the beam count, not the ends actually put on each beam.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Planning a set for a new quality step by step: ends, beams, cone length, yards to size, sets, bags and the yarn diameter behind the beam length.

questions.q: A quality has 120 ends per inch and a warp width of 60 in. How many total ends are there?
With 7,200 total ends and a limit of about 840 ends per beam, rounded up to an even number of beams, the set needs:
questions.explain: 7,200 ÷ 840 = 8.57, rounded up to the next even number gives 10 beams; 7,200 ÷ 10 = 720 ends per beam. Eight beams would exceed 840 ends each.

questions.q: How many yards of Ne 30 yarn does a 4.17 lb cone hold after 2 % wastage? Round to the nearest 10 yd.
Each weaver's beam of a quality is to be 2,500 yd and the quality runs on 8 looms. How many yards must be sized from each warper's beam of the set?
questions.explain: Yd to size = sized length × looms = 2,500 × 8 = 20,000 yd per warper's beam.

questions.q: A set of 10 warper's beams must each supply 20,000 yd, and one Ne 20 cone yields 68,655 yd. How many sets are required before rounding, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Cone yardage required = 20,000 × 10 = 200,000 yd per end; ÷ 68,655 = 2.91 sets, which rounds (with the 0.05 allowance) to 3 sets used.

questions.q: A quality has 720 ends per beam and uses 3 sets. How many 24-cone bags of yarn must be issued?
questions.explain: Bags = 720 × 3 ÷ 24 = 90 bags of 100 lb.

questions.q: Using d = 1/(26√Ne), what is the diameter of an Ne 20 yarn in inches, to four decimal places?

A weaver's beam has a yarn volume of 39,100 in³ and carries 8,064 ends of Ne 20 (d = 1/(26√20) in). Taking the yarn cross-section as π/4 × d², how many yards of warp fit on the beam? Round to the nearest yard.
The worksheet uses 2 sets of Ne 20 (68,655 yd per cone) for a set of 10 beams. How many yards does each warper's beam actually get?
questions.explain: Actual yd per beam = 68,655 × 2 ÷ 10 = 13,731 yd against the 13,911 yd planned — a little short, as the lecture notes.

questions.q: A creel holds 807 cones of 4.17 lb. How many pounds of yarn go into one set? Round to the nearest pound.
questions.explain: 807 × 4.17 = 3,365 lb per set, about 34 bags' worth.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions in the weaving planning office: issuing yarn, choosing cone sizes, dealing with short beams and changing counts.

questions.q: Row 3 of the worksheet calculates 2.03 sets but uses 2. What should the planner expect on the loom?
options: Each weaver's beam will be about 1.3 % shorter than the planned 2,319 yd
The looms will stop for lack of yarn
The cones will run out before the last beam
questions.explain: The whole set is simply warped a little shorter (13,731 instead of 13,911 yd per warper's beam), so every loom beam is proportionally shorter; nothing runs out.

questions.q: The store issues yarn for the 20×16 quality by total ends (8,064) × 2 sets ÷ 24 = 672 bags instead of 68. The consequence is:
options: About ten times too much yarn is drawn from the store
questions.explain: The creel holds only ends-per-beam cones (807); all 10 beams are warped from the same creel. Counting every beam's ends separately multiplies the issue by the number of beams.

questions.q: A quality works out at 4.80 sets and the planner uses 5. Compared with the worksheet's 2.03 → 2 case, the beams will be:
options: Slightly longer than planned, since the cones supply more than needed
Unaffected, because sets do not change beam length
questions.explain: Rounding up means the creel supplies 5 × 54,924 = 274,620 yd per end against 263,796 required, so the warper's beams can be made longer (27,462 yd against 26,380) or some yarn is left over.

questions.q: The spinner offers 2.5 lb cones instead of 4.17 lb. For the same quality and looms, the planner should expect:
options: More sets and more creel changes, since each cone supplies less length
The same sets but fewer bags
questions.explain: Length per cone falls in proportion to cone weight (2.5 ÷ 4.17), so about 1.67 times as many sets are needed; the total yarn is the same, but the warping is interrupted more often.

questions.q: If a quality moves from 6 looms to 12 looms, the ends per beam and the beams per set stay the same.
questions.explain: Beams and ends per beam depend on the total ends of the quality; more looms only mean more yards to size and so more sets and bags.

questions.q: The sizing department reports that the Ne 16 quality's beams only reach 2,198 yd while the Ne 20 beams of the same ends reach 2,748 yd. The planner should:
options: Accept it — a coarser yarn takes more space, so fewer yards fit in the same beam volume
Ask for more size to be applied
questions.explain: Beam length is proportional to Ne for a fixed volume: 2,748 × 16 ÷ 20 = 2,198 yd. The beams are full; the yarn is simply thicker.

questions.q: Which quality in the worksheet consumes the most bags of yarn, and why?
options: 20×10/118×52 — 744 ends per beam and 5 sets give 155 bags
questions.explain: Bags = ends per beam × sets ÷ 24: 744 × 5 ÷ 24 = 155. The 128×60 quality has more ends but only 2 sets (6 looms), giving 68 bags.

questions.q: A new quality has 9,000 total ends. Keeping to about 840 ends per beam and an even beam count, how many beams should the set have?
questions.explain: 9,000 ÷ 840 = 10.7, so 11 beams are needed and the even rule makes it 12 beams of 750 ends. Ten beams would carry 900 ends each, over the limit.

questions.q: Yarn arrives in 50 lb bags of 12 cones instead of 100 lb bags of 24. The bag formula should become:
questions.explain: The divisor is the number of cones per bag; with 12 cones a bag, twice as many bags are needed for the same cones.

questions.q: The lecture's original worksheet read sized-beam lengths from a maximum-volume table rather than computing them. The computed 2,319 yd and the table's 2,320 yd differ because:
options: The table rounds to the nearest 10 yd and uses a slightly different diameter constant
questions.explain: Both come from the same beam volume and yarn diameter; the small difference is rounding. The lecture says it read the same figures from the table on its second sheet.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder set-size reasoning: the effect of wastage and count, rounding of sets, shortfalls in yards and the mistakes that double the yarn issued.

questions.q: If wastage rises from 2 % to 4 %, how many yards does a 4.17 lb cone of Ne 20 yield? Round to the nearest yard.
questions.explain: 70,056 × 0.96 = 67,253.76 ≈ 67,254 yd, about 1,400 yd less than at 2 % wastage.

questions.q: Row 8 of the worksheet gives a sized-beam length of 2,748 yd for 6,804 ends of Ne 20. Keeping the same ends and beam volume, what length would Ne 16 give? Round to the nearest yard.
questions.explain: Length is proportional to Ne: 2,748 × 16 ÷ 20 = 2,198 yd, exactly row 7's figure.

questions.q: The worksheet plans 13,911 yd per warper's beam but 2 sets supply only 13,731 yd. What is the shortfall as a percentage of the plan, to one decimal place?
questions.explain: 180 ÷ 13,911 = 1.29 % ≈ 1.3 % — small enough for the lecture to round 2.03 sets down to 2.

questions.q: A quality calculates to 2.06 sets. With the worksheet's 0.05 allowance the sets used are:
questions.explain: ROUNDUP(2.06 − 0.05) = ROUNDUP(2.01) = 3; only a fraction of 0.05 or less is absorbed by making the beams shorter.

questions.q: 68 bags of 100 lb are issued for a set plan that actually needs 807 cones × 2 sets × 4.17 lb. How many pounds of yarn are left over? Round to the nearest pound.
questions.explain: Needed = 807 × 2 × 4.17 = 6,730 lb; issued 6,800 lb; surplus about 70 lb — the part-bag from rounding 67.25 bags up to 68.

questions.q: A student computes sets as sized length per beam × looms ÷ length per cone and forgets to multiply by beams. For the 20×16 quality the result is:
options: 0.20 sets instead of 2.03, ten times too few
questions.explain: 13,911 ÷ 68,655 = 0.20; the cones must supply every beam of the set, so the yardage must be multiplied by the 10 beams to reach 139,111 yd and 2.03 sets.

questions.q: Two qualities have the same total ends and beam volume: one is Ne 20 on 12 looms, the other Ne 30 on 12 looms. Compared with the Ne 20 quality, the Ne 30 quality needs:
options: The same number of sets, since the longer beam and the longer cone cancel out
questions.explain: Sized length per beam rises in proportion to Ne, and so does the length per cone; their ratio, and hence the sets, is unchanged. Bags follow sets, so they are unchanged too.

questions.q: For a fixed beam volume, halving the number of ends on the beam doubles the length of warp it can hold.
questions.explain: Length = volume ÷ (ends × cross-section): with half the ends the same volume holds twice the length. This is why the narrow 51-in 128×44 quality gets 2,864 yd against 2,319 yd for the 63-in 128×60.

questions.q: A quality of 7,200 ends of Ne 30 (d = 1/(26√30) in) is beamed on a beam of 39,100 in³ yarn volume. Taking the cross-section as π/4 × d², how many yards fit? Round to the nearest 10 yd.
A planner wants fewer creel changes on a 12-loom quality that needs 4.8 sets. Which change would reduce the sets required?
options: Shorter weaver's beams, so less yardage is needed per set
Finer yarn at the same cone weight
questions.explain: Sets = beams × looms × sized length ÷ cone length; shorter beams cut the numerator. Finer yarn lengthens both cone and beam and cancels out; more looms or smaller cones increase sets. Shorter beams, however, mean more beam changes on the loom — the trade-off of set-size planning.
